title: ReSFlow: Rectifying Categorical Flows on Statistical Manifolds for One-Step Generation

paper.title: ReSFlow: Rectifying Categorical Flows on Statistical Manifolds for One-Step Generation
paper.abstract: Abstract Generative modeling for discrete data has been significantly advanced by learning continuous vector fields on the statistical manifolds to transport simple priors to target discrete distributions. However, because these continuous-time flows are not constrained to follow geodesics on the statistical manifold, thereby requiring multi-step numerical integration for simulation and leading to substantial computational costs during inference. In this work, drawing inspiration from the “straight and fast” properties of Rectified Flow in continuous Euclidean space, we propose the Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow) model, which enables one-step categorical generation on statistical manifolds by explicitly learning geodesic trajectories that adhere to the intrinsic Riemannian geometry. By rectifying the flow on the statistical manifold, we theoretically guarantee that trajectories between prior and target distributions approximate geodesics. This rectification significantly reduces the transport cost by aligning the learned trajectories directly along geodesics on the statistical manifold, allowing the model to map pure noise to target discrete data in a single step. Through extensive experiments on diverse real-world generative tasks, ranging from image and text to biological domains, we demonstrate ReSFlow’s superior one-step generation quality, which truly embodies geodesically optimal and rapid categorical generation. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaohuanjia/ReSFlow .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Generative modeling has advanced rapidly, with diffusion and flow-based methods achieving state-of-the-art performance across continuous domains such as image synthesis Dao et al. (2023) ; Lipman et al. (2023a) , molecule and protein design Campbell et al. (2024) ; Zaghen et al. (2025) ; Huguet et al. (2024) , and sequence generation Davis et al. (2024b) ; Shaul et al. (2024) . A key idea is to learn continuous-time dynamics, especially through flow matching, which formulates ODEs with continuous vector fields and provides a simulation-free, theoretically grounded training framework Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden (2023) . However, extending these methods to discrete data—common in NLP, drug discovery, and protein engineering—remains difficult, since discrete variables do not have the differentiable structure required by continuous flows. Most existing flow-based generative models for discrete data act directly on the native discrete space by optimizing the categorical probabilities of tokens ( Gat et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Yoo et al., 2025 ; Stark et al., 2024 ) . Rather than operating strictly within this discrete realm, a promising direction maps discrete variables to statistical manifolds, treating each categorical distribution as a point on the probability simplex with Riemannian geometry Cheng et al. (2024) . This allows smooth vector fields and continuous-time flows to transport priors to target discrete distributions, bridging continuous generative modeling and discrete data synthesis. However, a critical limitation persists: The learned ODE trajectories deviate from geodesics because the conditional vector fields arising from independent couplings of prior and target samples yield a mixture of intersecting geodesics that, once marginalized, produce highly curved aggregate flows not aligned with any single geodesic path Cheng et al. (2025) . Simulating these tortuous trajectories demands multi-step numerical integration with fine temporal discretization, incurring substantial computational overhead during inference. This stands in stark contrast to the desiderata of modern generative systems, where rapid, ideally single-step, sampling is essential for scalable deployment. The fundamental tension between the geometric complexity of learned flows and the practical need for efficient generation thus constitutes a major bottleneck for categorical generative models. In the continuous Euclidean setting, an elegant solution to this problem has emerged through the concept of Rectified Flow Liu et al. (2023) . Rectified Flow enforces straight-line trajectories between paired noise and data samples, yielding flows that are both geometrically simple and computationally efficient to simulate. The resulting “straight and fast” property enables high-quality generation with very few or even a single integration step, dramatically accelerating inference. Naturally, one might ask: can we bring the same benefits of trajectory rectification to categorical generation on statistical manifolds? The answer, however, is far from straightforward. The probability simplex, when equipped with the Fisher-Rao metric Rao (1992) , forms a Riemannian manifold whose geometry is fundamentally non-Euclidean. Straight paths in ambient Euclidean space do not respect the intrinsic curvature of this manifold—they may leave the simplex, violate probability constraints, or deviate substantially from the true shortest paths. In this curved geometric setting, the natural analogue of a “straight path” is a geodesic: the length-minimizing curve that faithfully adheres to the manifold’s intrinsic Riemannian structure. Consequently, achieving efficient one-step categorical generation requires not Euclidean straightening, but rather a fundamentally geometric approach that aligns learned trajectories with the geodesics of the underlying statistical manifold. In this work, we propose Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow), a framework that enables one-step discrete data generation by rectifying flows on statistical manifolds. The core idea is to map data from the probability simplex onto the positive orthant of the hypersphere via their natural diffeomorphism, and then perform flow rectification in this spherical space where geodesics admit closed-form great-circle expressions. By iteratively recoupling the learned ODE marginals and retraining the vector field on the hypersphere, ReSFlow progressively straightens transport paths toward geodesics, reducing both transport cost and path curvature. Extensive evaluations across vision, NLP, and bioinformatics benchmarks demonstrate that ReSFlow, requiring only a single sampling step, matches or outperforms state-of-the-art methods that rely on hundreds of steps.

sections.heading: 3 Method
sections.text: As discussed above, the extension of rectified flow to statistical manifolds poses additional challenges, as the model needs to be fully aware of the intrinsic geometry induced by the Fisher information metric to properly define and straighten the ODE trajectories. In particular, the velocity field estimation and the evolution of marginal distributions—both central to the rectified flow framework—must be reformulated to respect the curvature and geometric structure of the statistical manifold. To address these challenges, we propose the Rectified Categorical Flow model, which reflows and straightens the ODE trajectories along geodesics on a mapped hyperspherical manifold. Figure 1: Overview of Spherical Rectified Flow. Top: Standard reflow straightens linear paths on the simplex, but their corresponding spherical geodesics still intersect, preventing one-step sampling. Bottom: We perform reflow directly on the sphere 𝕊 + \mathbb{S}_{+} . This straightens the geodesics themselves to be non-intersecting, ensuring faithful one-step generation.

sections.heading: 4.1 Experimental setup
sections.text: Our proposed ReSFlow models arbitrary distributions over categorical probability measures and enables one-step sampling via geodesic rectification on the statistical manifold. We first validate this property on a synthetic Swiss-roll distribution on the simplex, and then evaluate ReSFlow on real-world discrete generation tasks, including binarized MNIST image generation, character-level Text8 modeling, and conditional promoter DNA sequence design. Our primary comparison is with SFM Cheng et al. (2024) , which achieves state-of-the-art performance on these benchmarks. The additional baselines reported in that work rely on multi-step sampling and do not outperform SFM; we therefore do not repeat them here. To disentangle the effects of geometry and rectification, we compare four controlled variants: Linear Flow Matching (LinearFM) Cheng et al. (2024) , which uses Euclidean linear interpolation on the simplex; Statistical Flow Matching (SFM), which maps the simplex to the positive orthant of the hypersphere and follows spherical geodesics; Rectified Linear Flow Matching (R-LFM), which applies rectification in the Euclidean setting; and Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow), our proposed spherical reflow model. This 2 × 2 2\times 2 design separates the choice of geometry, Euclidean versus spherical, from the effect of rectification. Moreover, we also compare with SOTA flow-based one-step generation ReDi Yoo et al. (2025) , which rectifies the flow trajectories of continuous token embeddings in Euclidean space. The fundamental difference between their setting and ours lies in the data preprocessing requirement. While their method relies on an external pre-trained model to tokenize the input data, our ReSFlow operates as a fully end-to-end framework directly on the raw data space. By bypassing the discrete tokenization step, our approach is highly advantageous for domains and modalities where well-established pre-trained tokenizers are unavailable. Due to the absence of well-established tokenizers for binarized MNIST and promoter DNA sequences, we restrict our comparison with ReDi solely to the Text8, where characters are tokenized using the GPT-2 tokenizer. We evaluate all methods under different numbers of function evaluations (NFE). For sample-quality metrics such as FID Heusel et al. (2017) and SP-MSE, we report both one-step generation with NFE = 1 =1 and accurate ODE simulation using the adaptive Dormand–Prince 5 (Dopri5) solver Dormand and Prince (1980) . For the Swiss-roll benchmark, we report only Dopri5-based results, including ODE-based NLL and Dopri5 sampling time. Likelihood-based metrics are evaluated only with ODE integration: NLL estimation uses the continuous-time change-of-variables formula and therefore requires accurate integration of the learned dynamics, while a single Euler or exponential-map step does not yield reliable likelihoods. For Text8, BPC is computed from the variational integral formulation rather than generated samples, and is therefore not tied to one-step sampling. Thus, one-step sampling measures fast generation quality, whereas ODE-based integration evaluates NLL and BPC. We also report wall-clock sampling time for binarized MNIST, promoter sequence design, and Swiss-roll to quantify practical runtime , but omit timing for Text8, since the reported BPC metric is based on likelihood evaluation rather than sample generation. Detailed architectures and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix .

sections.heading: 4.2 Toy Example: Swiss Roll on the Simplex
sections.text: We first evaluate ReSFlow on a Swiss-roll distribution on the 2 2 -simplex as a low-dimensional geometric sanity check. Following Cheng et al. Cheng et al. (2024) , we normalize a two-dimensional Swiss roll and embed it into the simplex by setting μ 3 = 1 − μ 1 − μ 2 \mu_{3}=1-\mu_{1}-\mu_{2} . All methods use the same time-dependent MLP and training budget. LinearFM and R-LFM use Euclidean interpolation on the simplex; SFM and ReSFlow use the square-root map with spherical geodesic interpolation on 𝕊 + \mathbb{S}_{+} . This controlled comparison separates the effect of geometry from the effect of rectification. As shown in Table , ReSFlow achieves an NLL of − 2.25 -2.25 , improving over LinearFM ( − 1.88 -1.88 ) and R-LFM ( − 1.87 -1.87 ), and remains competitive with SFM ( − 2.38 -2.38 ). It also attains the fastest ODE sampling time among all methods, reducing the runtime from 0.0679 0.0679 s for SFM to 0.0361 0.0361 s. This indicates that ReSFlow preserves the geometric advantage of Fisher–Rao geodesics and enabling efficient ODE generation. The samples in Fig. further illustrate the role of spherical reflow under one-step sampling. Non-rectified LinearFM and SFM fail to recover the Swiss-roll structure in the one-step setting, because their marginal vector fields average over many crossing conditional paths, producing curved trajectories that are poorly approximated by a single update. Euclidean reflow improves one-step behavior relative to LinearFM, but it still rectifies paths under the wrong geometry, leading to samples that only partially capture the target structure. ReSFlow instead performs reflow directly on the hypersphere, aligning the learned trajectories with Fisher–Rao geodesics and producing the most faithful one-step samples. This supports the central claim that geometry and rectification are complementary: the hyperspherical formulation provides the correct transport geometry, while reflow reduces trajectory curvature for accurate one-step sampling. sections.heading: 4.3 Binarized MNIST
sections.text: We next evaluate on binarized MNIST to test whether the geometric and rectification effects observed in the Swiss-roll experiment extend to high-dimensional discrete generation. Each image is modeled as a collection of Bernoulli categorical variables, so good samples require both local binary consistency and global digit structure. This benchmark therefore allows us to examine two questions in a realistic setting: whether Fisher–Rao geometry improves categorical transport, and whether reflow makes the learned dynamics accurate under NFE = 1 sampling. Following the evaluation protocol above, we compare adaptive ODE sampling with Euler one-step generation. Table reports mean FID and wall-clock sampling time over three random seeds. Under adaptive ODE sampling, SFM achieves the best FID, confirming that spherical geodesic interpolation provides a stronger reference geometry than Euclidean interpolation for binary categorical data. ReSFlow is slightly worse than SFM in this full-ODE regime, but remains competitive and is the fastest ODE-based method. Under one-step sampling, non-rectified LinearFM and SFM degrade substantially, indicating that their learned trajectories are too curved to be approximated by a single update. Rectification alleviates this issue, and ReSFlow achieves the best one-step FID by performing reflow under the hyperspherical Fisher–Rao geometry. Compared with SFM under accurate ODE sampling, one-step ReSFlow achieves an orders-of-magnitude improvement in sampling speed ( 0.452 0.452 vs. 112.81 112.81 seconds per 1,000 samples), while incurring only a mild and acceptable degradation in FID ( 5.973 5.973 vs. 4.748 4.748 ). sections.heading: 4.4 Text8
sections.text: We further evaluate ReSFlow on character-level language modeling with Text8 Mahoney (2011) , where each token is a categorical variable and the sequence distribution is substantially more structured than the toy and image settings. This experiment is designed to test whether the proposed manifold-aware rectification remains effective for high-entropy discrete sequences with a larger alphabet and stronger contextual dependencies. Since text generation is typically evaluated by predictive coding efficiency, we report bits per character (BPC), which naturally reflects whether the learned categorical transport is efficient and sufficiently well aligned with the data distribution: a lower BPC indicates that the model assigns higher probability to the observed character sequences and induces less distorted transport over categorical states. Since BPC is evaluated from the continuous-time likelihood, it requires ODE integration; we therefore report only ODE-based BPC in Table . Table shows that the choice of geometry has a pronounced effect on categorical sequence modeling. SFM substantially improves over LinearFM, reducing BPC from 2.154 2.154 to 1.830 1.830 , which supports the importance of modeling categorical data under the Fisher–Rao geometry rather than using Euclidean interpolation on the simplex. Moreover, R-LFM performs worse than LinearFM, increasing BPC to 3.267 3.267 . This agrees with the failure mode discussed in Section : rectifying paths in the ambient Euclidean space optimizes the wrong notion of straightness and transport cost. The effect is especially harmful for character-level sequences, where local geometric errors can accumulate over many categorical variables and time steps, ultimately degrading the likelihood. Furthermore, although ReDi leverages pre-trained token embeddings to map discrete data into a continuous space, its Euclidean rectification only yields a BPC of 2.306 2.306 , exposing a substantial performance gap compared to our ReSFlow ( 1.261 1.261 ). This sharp contrast underscores that relying on pre-trained continuous representations cannot compensate for geometric mismatches, proving the necessity of optimizing discrete data strictly within its suitable intrinsic space. By performing rectification under the correct manifold geometry, ReSFlow achieves the best overall BPC, confirming the effectiveness of our approach. Compared with binarized MNIST, Text8 has a larger categorical alphabet and richer sequential dependencies, so accumulated geometric errors are more likely to affect the final likelihood. By combining hyperspherical statistical-manifold modeling with reflow, ReSFlow preserves the intrinsic geometric advantage of SFM while further aligning the learned trajectories with geodesic transport on the manifold. These results support our design choice: the manifold formulation captures the proper geometry of discrete data, and rectification should be performed within that geometry to obtain efficient and reliable categorical generation. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We proposed Rectified Statistical Flow (ReSFlow), a principled generative framework for discrete data that performs flow matching directly on the probability simplex under its natural spherical geometry. By proposing a reflow procedure in the spherical space via the square-root parameterization, ReSFlow respects the intrinsic Riemannian structure of categorical distributions while admitting closed-form conditional velocity fields. We further established a theoretical guarantee on the straightening rate of iterative spherical rectification, and demonstrated the effectiveness of ReSFlow over existing baselines across diverse discrete generation tasks. As future work, the straightening property of ReSFlow naturally lends itself to single-step generation on other spherical data, such as unit-norm embeddings, directional statistics, and rotation-valued representations.

sections.heading: Appendix A Statistical Manifold of Categorical Distributions and the Spherical Projection
sections.text: To formulate continuous-time generative dynamics for discrete data, a natural approach is to consider the n n -class categorical distributions as points lying on the ( n − 1 ) (n-1) -dimensional probability simplex Δ \Delta . Geometrically, Δ \Delta can be treated as a Riemannian manifold, known as the statistical manifold, where the intrinsic geometry is governed by the Fisher Information Metric. For a distribution μ ∈ Δ \mu\in\Delta (where ∑ i = 1 μ i = 1 \sum_{i=1}\mu_{i}=1 and μ i ≥ 0 \mu_{i}\geq 0 ) and tangent vectors u , v u,v at μ \mu , the Fisher inner product is defined as: ⟨ u , v ⟩ μ = ∑ i = 1 u i ​ v i μ i . \langle u,v\rangle_{\mu}=\sum_{i=1}\frac{u_{i}v_{i}}{\mu_{i}}. (15)

sections.heading: The Boundary Illness.
sections.text: While the Fisher metric elegantly captures the information geometry of probability distributions, reveals a critical flaw for generative modeling: the inner product becomes ill-defined on the boundary of the simplex. As any probability mass μ i → 0 \mu_{i}\to 0 , the denominator causes the metric to diverge. In discrete generation tasks, the target data points are typically deterministic, represented as one-hot vectors. These one-hot vectors lie exactly on the sharp corners (boundaries) of the simplex. Consequently, performing flow matching or integrating vector fields directly on Δ \Delta using the Fisher metric leads to severe numerical instability and singularities near the targets.

sections.heading: Necessity of the Spherical Projection.
sections.text: To circumvent this boundary illness while preserving the intrinsic geometry, we introduce the square-root diffeomorphism: π : Δ → 𝕊 + , μ i ↦ x i = μ i . \pi:\Delta\to\mathbb{S}_{+},\quad\mu_{i}\mapsto x_{i}=\sqrt{\mu_{i}}. (16) Since ∑ i = 1 μ i = 1 \sum_{i=1}\mu_{i}=1 , it naturally follows that ∑ i = 1 x i = 1 \sum_{i=1}x_{i}=1 . This transformation smoothly maps the original probability simplex to the positive orthant of the unit sphere 𝕊 + \mathbb{S}_{+} . Under this mapping, the intrinsic geometry of the statistical manifold is beautifully preserved up to a constant factor. Specifically, the geodesic distance d cat d_{\text{cat}} on the simplex is strictly proportional to the standard great-circle distance d S d_{S} on the sphere: d cat ​ ( μ , ν ) = 2 ​ d 𝕊 ​ ( π ⁡ ( μ ) , π ⁡ ( ν ) ) , d_{\text{cat}}(\mu,\nu)=2d_{\mathbb{S}}(\pi(\mu),\pi(\nu)), (17) where d 𝕊 ​ ( x , y ) = arccos ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 x i ​ y i ) d_{\mathbb{S}}(x,y)=\arccos(\sum_{i=1}x_{i}y_{i}) for x , y ∈ 𝕊 + x,y\in\mathbb{S}_{+} . This indicates that we can seamlessly perform geometric operations on the unit sphere instead of the simplex. Beyond preserving the distance metric, this transformation fundamentally resolves the boundary illness. For a point x ∈ 𝕊 + x\in\mathbb{S}_{+} , its tangent space is given by T x ​ 𝕊 + = { u ~ ∈ ℝ ∣ ∑ i = 1 x i ​ u ~ i = 0 } T_{x}\mathbb{S}_{+}=\{\tilde{u}\in\mathbb{R}\mid\sum_{i=1}x_{i}\tilde{u}_{i}=0\} . sections.heading: Appendix B Related Work
sections.text: Flow matching was originally proposed for continuous domains as an alternative to diffusion, learning transport along a prescribed probability path [ 21 , 8 , 15 ] . Extending this idea to discrete spaces is more challenging, since the dynamics evolve over categorical distributions rather than Euclidean variables. Related work has modeled discrete denoising in continuous time using continuous-time Markov chains (CTMCs), bridging diffusion-style methods and discrete data [ 22 ] . Building on this perspective, Discrete Flow Matching [ 9 ] extends flow matching to discrete generation, while subsequent methods further refine the geometry and path design, including Fisher Flow Matching [ 23 ] and Dirichlet Flow Matching [ 12 ] . Compared with discrete diffusion, which typically learns reverse transitions, these approaches emphasize direct probability transport. Among them, Statistical Flow Matching (SFM) [ 13 ] is particularly appealing, as it formulates categorical generation on the simplex as a statistical manifold, better respecting the geometry of categorical distributions while avoiding explicit CTMC jump-rate parameterization. This provides a cleaner and often more stable framework for discrete generation, and thus serves as the foundation of our model. Flow-based models can generate high-quality discrete samples, but inference is often costly, typically requiring tens to hundreds of function evaluations. Moreover, most one- or few-step generative methods focus on continuous data [ 15 , 24 , 14 , 25 ] ; in discrete spaces, fast sampling has been explored mainly within diffusion-based frameworks through distillation or specialized acceleration schemes [ 26 , 27 , 10 , 28 ] . Flow matching is often considered more suitable for low-step generation because it learns transport dynamics rather than local denoising and allows the design of straighter probability paths, e.g., rectified or OT-inspired flows. Its deterministic ODE formulation may therefore be easier to compress into a few updates, although standard flow matching is not inherently one-step. Recently, ReDi [ 11 ] extended rectified flow to discrete spaces via iterative reflow. However, this approach—like many continuous relaxation methods for discrete spaces—heavily requires pre-trained token embeddings to function, restricting its applicability when training purely from scratch. Moreover, the extension is performed entirely in Euclidean space, ignoring the intrinsic Riemannian geometry of the probability simplex. As a result, linear interpolation paths are not true geodesics on the statistical manifold, leading to suboptimal transport costs and trajectories that are inherently harder to straighten through reflow. Consequently, ReDi’s practical advantages over standard discrete flow matching remain less clear-cut than those of rectified flow in continuous settings.

sections.heading: Appendix E Experimental Setup
sections.text: In this appendix, we provide dataset-specific implementation details for all benchmarks. Since the network architectures and training protocols differ across datasets, we describe the data processing, model architecture, and optimization setup separately for each benchmark. Unless otherwise specified, all rectified variants use a single reflow iteration, and all reflow models are initialized from the previous checkpoint and fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch. We summarize sampling procedures and evaluation metrics at the end of this section.

sections.heading: Dataset and preprocessing.
sections.text: We follow the Swiss-roll-on-simplex construction used in prior categorical flow-matching work. The data lie on the 2 2 -simplex with K = 3 K=3 categories, i.e., each sample is a probability vector μ ∈ Δ \mu\in\Delta . We generate 1000 1000 samples and use the resulting fixed empirical distribution as the target distribution q q for this toy experiment. Since this benchmark is used as a geometric sanity check, we do not use a separate validation or test split. Reported likelihoods are evaluated on the same fixed empirical distribution and should be interpreted as relative comparisons among methods rather than as generalization metrics. The construction maps a two-dimensional Swiss roll to the simplex as follows. Let x x and y y denote the two Swiss-roll coordinates. We first shift each coordinate by subtracting its batchwise minimum and adding a padding constant pad = 1.0 \mathrm{pad}=1.0 . We then define M = max i ⁡ ( x i + y i ) + pad , z i = M − ( x i + y i ) , M=\max_{i}(x_{i}+y_{i})+\mathrm{pad},\qquad z_{i}=M-(x_{i}+y_{i}), and obtain the simplex point by normalizing μ i = ( x i , y i , z i ) M . \mu_{i}=\frac{(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i})}{M}. This construction ensures that all coordinates are nonnegative and sum to one. There is no additional dataset-level ϵ \epsilon -smoothing parameter; numerical stabilization inside the flow model uses ϵ = 10 \epsilon=10 where needed. The prior distribution p 0 p_{0} is sampled on the simplex by drawing independent exponential random variables, normalizing them to sum to one, applying a small clamp for numerical stability, and renormalizing. The target distribution q q is the empirical distribution over the 1000 1000 generated Swiss-roll samples. Unless otherwise stated, we use random seed 42 42 for data and model initialization, and seed 0 0 for generating reflow pairs.

sections.heading: Model architecture.
sections.text: For this benchmark, all methods use the same MLP vector-field backbone. The input has per-position dimension 3 3 and tensor shape ( B , 1 , 3 ) (B,1,3) , and the network outputs a vector field with the same per-position dimension. The hidden dimension is set to 128 128 . The encoder consists of an input branch, a time branch, and a fusion head. The input branch maps the current state through two linear layers with ReLU activation. The time branch applies two linear layers to a sinusoidal time-step embedding. The time embedding dimension is 128 128 . The resulting state and time features are concatenated and passed through a fusion MLP with three linear layers and ReLU activations to produce the final vector-field prediction. We do not use dropout or normalization layers in this toy architecture. All compared methods use this same MLP backbone in the Swiss-roll experiment. The methods differ only in their geometry and flow construction. LinearFM and R-LFM use Euclidean interpolation and projection on the simplex, whereas SFM and ReSFlow use the square-root map and spherical geometry on 𝕊 + \mathbb{S}_{+} . Tangent-space projection is applied as described in Appendix .

sections.heading: Training protocol.
sections.text: For the initial flow-matching model, we train with Adam using learning rate 10 10 and no weight decay. Since the dataset contains only 1000 1000 points, we use full-batch training with batch size 1000 1000 . Each model is trained for 2000 2000 epochs, corresponding to one parameter update per epoch. We do not use learning-rate scheduling, warmup, gradient clipping, or exponential moving average for this toy experiment. For the reflow variants, we use one reflow iteration. In both R-LFM and ReSFlow, the reflow model is initialized from the previous checkpoint and then fine-tuned, rather than trained from scratch. At the beginning of the reflow stage, we generate 10,000 10{,}000 recoupled endpoint pairs in batches of 256 256 using ODE sampling from t = 0 t=0 to t = 1 t=1 with solver tolerances atol = 10 \mathrm{atol}=10 and rtol = 10 \mathrm{rtol}=10 . The resulting model is trained for 2000 2000 epochs using mini-batches of 256 256 recoupled pairs. The two methods differ only in the geometry used for reflow: R-LFM performs Euclidean/straight-line reflow in the simplex geometry, whereas ReSFlow uses spherical tangent reflow under the square-root map.

sections.heading: Dataset and preprocessing.
sections.text: We use the static binarized MNIST dataset with the standard 50,000 / 10,000 / 10,000 50{,}000/10{,}000/10{,}000 train/validation/test split. Each image has spatial resolution 28 × 28 28\times 28 . The original data are represented as 784 784 binary variables, and we treat each pixel as a categorical variable with K = 2 K=2 categories. Concretely, each binary pixel value x ∈ { 0 , 1 } x\in\{0,1\} is represented by the two-dimensional simplex coordinate ( x , 1 − x ) (x,1-x) . Thus, the model input is arranged as a tensor of shape ( 28 , 28 , 2 ) (28,28,2) . The prior distribution p 0 p_{0} is sampled independently at each pixel location by drawing exponential random variables for the two categories, normalizing them onto the simplex, applying a small clamp for numerical stability, and renormalizing. The data are not smoothed or dequantized. Unless otherwise specified, numerical stabilization inside the flow model uses ϵ = 10 \epsilon=10 . No additional image preprocessing is applied. In the convolutional vector-field network, the simplex-valued input is internally rescaled from [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] to [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] before the first convolutional layer.

sections.heading: Model architecture.
sections.text: For binarized MNIST, we use a convolutional vector-field predictor. The input and output tensors both have shape ( B , 28 , 28 , 2 ) (B,28,28,2) , where the last dimension corresponds to the two categorical states of each pixel. Internally, the categorical dimension is treated as the channel dimension for convolutional processing. All methods compared on binarized MNIST use the same convolutional backbone unless otherwise stated. The differences between methods are in the geometric parameterization and the reflow procedure. LinearFM and R-LFM use Euclidean/simplex geometry, whereas SFM and ReSFlow use the square-root map and spherical geometry on 𝕊 + \mathbb{S}_{+} . The shared backbone uses four residual stages, four top-down refinement blocks, ELU activations, InstanceNorm++ normalization, and additive sinusoidal time embeddings with embedding dimension 128 128 .

sections.heading: Training protocol.
sections.text: For the base model, we train with Adam using learning rate 3 × 10 3\times 10 , weight decay 0 0 , and batch size 256 256 . Models are trained for 100,000 100{,}000 optimization steps. We use a reduce-on-plateau learning-rate schedule with decay factor 0.5 0.5 , patience 10 10 , and minimum learning rate 10 10 . No warmup is used. We clip the global gradient norm to 100 100 . No exponential moving average is used. Unless otherwise specified, the random seed is set to 42 42 . For rectified models, we generate recoupled endpoint pairs from the previously trained model by ODE sampling from t = 0 t=0 to t = 1 t=1 with solver tolerances atol = 10 \mathrm{atol}=10 and rtol = 10 \mathrm{rtol}=10 . The rectified model is initialized from the previous checkpoint and fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch. For each method, we generate 50,000 50{,}000 recoupled pairs in batches of 256 256 and train the rectified model for 100,000 100{,}000 optimization steps with batch size 256 256 and learning rate 10 10 . ReSFlow uses spherical tangent reflow, whereas R-LFM uses Euclidean/simplex reflow. Experiments were run on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 GPU with CUDA 13.0 and PyTorch 2.7.0.

sections.heading: Dataset and preprocessing.
sections.text: We use the Text8 character-level language modeling benchmark. We follow the standard character-level Text8 split: the first 90 90 M characters are used for training, the next 5 5 M for validation, and the final 5 5 M for testing. The vocabulary consists of the 26 26 lowercase English letters and the space character, resulting in 27 27 symbols. Each character is mapped to an integer token. We use a sequence length of 256 256 . Each training example is a contiguous window of 256 256 characters. Tokens are represented as one-hot vectors, so each sample has shape ( 256 , 27 ) (256,27) , and a mini-batch has shape ( B , 256 , 27 ) (B,256,27) . No additional text normalization, smoothing, or dequantization is applied beyond the character-level encoding. The prior distribution p 0 p_{0} is sampled independently at each sequence position by drawing exponential random variables over the 27 27 categories, normalizing them onto the simplex, applying a small clamp for numerical stability, and renormalizing. Unless otherwise specified, numerical stabilization inside the flow model uses ϵ = 10 \epsilon=10 .

sections.heading: Model architecture.
sections.text: For Text8, all methods using the DiT backbone share the same architecture unless otherwise specified. The vector-field predictor operates on sequences of length 256 256 with vocabulary size 27 27 , using 12 12 transformer blocks with hidden dimension 768 768 , 12 12 attention heads, MLP expansion ratio 4 4 , GELU feed-forward activations, SiLU time-conditioning activations, dropout 0.1 0.1 , layer normalization, and rotary positional embeddings. Time is encoded by a sinusoidal timestep embedding of size 256 256 followed by a two-layer MLP producing a 128 128 -dimensional conditioning vector, which is injected into each block through adaptive layer normalization via shift, scale, and gate parameters. The final layer outputs a 27 27 -dimensional vector-field prediction at each sequence position.

sections.heading: Training protocol.
sections.text: In the training stage, the base DiT model is trained with AdamW using learning rate 3 × 10 3\times 10 , weight decay 0.1 0.1 , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , and β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 . We train for 750,000 750{,}000 optimization steps with global batch size 512 512 , using linear warmup for the first 1000 1000 steps followed by a reduce-on-plateau learning-rate schedule with minimum learning rate 10 10 . The global gradient norm is clipped to 1.0 1.0 . In the reflow stage, recoupled endpoint pairs are generated from the previous model by ODE sampling from t = 0 t=0 to t = 1 t=1 with tolerances atol = 10 \mathrm{atol}=10 and rtol = 10 \mathrm{rtol}=10 . The reflow model is initialized from the previous checkpoint and fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch. We generate 100,000 100{,}000 recoupled pairs in batches of 256 256 and train the reflow model for 40,000 40{,}000 optimization steps with batch size 256 256 and learning rate 4 × 10 4\times 10 . ReSFlow uses the spherical parameterization induced by the square-root map, while R-LFM uses the Euclidean reflow parameterization. Training was performed on 4 4 NVIDIA A800 GPUs and took approximately 6 6 days.

sections.heading: Dataset and preprocessing.
sections.text: We use the promoter sequence design dataset from the official Zenodo data package, which includes the GRCh38 reference genome, FANTOM transcription start site (TSS) annotations, CAGE signal tracks, blacklist regions, and the pre-trained Sei model for downstream evaluation. Each example is a 1024 1024 bp DNA sequence over the alphabet { A , C , G , T } \{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{G},\mathrm{T}\} , represented as a one-hot tensor in ℝ \mathbb{R} ; ambiguous bases are encoded as the uniform vector ( 1 / 4 , 1 / 4 , 1 / 4 , 1 / 4 ) (1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4) . The data split is chromosome-based: after taking the first 100,000 100{,}000 FANTOM TSS entries, chromosomes chr8 \mathrm{chr8} and chr9 \mathrm{chr9} are used for testing, chr10 \mathrm{chr10} for validation, and all remaining chromosomes for training. The conditioning signal is the FANTOM CAGE signal aligned to the same 1024 1024 bp window as the DNA sequence. We use the plus-strand CAGE channel as a per-position scalar condition, giving a conditioning tensor in ℝ \mathbb{R} . During training, the TSS position is randomly shifted by an offset sampled from { − 10 , … , 10 } \{-10,\ldots,10\} before extracting the sequence and signal window; no offset is used for validation or testing. The flow prior p 0 p_{0} is the categorical simplex prior, sampled independently at each sequence position and normalized to match the 1024 × 4 1024\times 4 sequence representation, while the target distribution is the empirical distribution of one-hot promoter sequences paired with their CAGE conditions.

sections.heading: Model architecture.
sections.text: The vector-field predictor for promoter design is a one-dimensional dilated convolutional residual network. It takes the current categorical state x t ∈ ℝ x_{t}\in\mathbb{R} and the CAGE condition c ∈ ℝ c\in\mathbb{R} , concatenates them into a 5 5 -channel input, and maps them to 256 256 hidden channels with an initial kernel-size- 9 9 convolution. The backbone contains 20 20 residual convolutional blocks with 256 256 channels, kernel size 9 9 , GroupNorm with one group, Swish activations, and additive time conditioning. The dilation pattern is ( 1 , 1 , 4 , 16 , 64 ) (1,1,4,16,64) repeated four times. Time is embedded with Gaussian Fourier features followed by a linear layer and SiLU activation, producing a 256 256 -dimensional embedding that is added to each block after projection. The CAGE signal is not separately encoded, but is injected only by input concatenation. A final 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolutional head with GELU activation maps 256 → 256 → 4 256\to 256\to 4 , yielding a four-channel vector-field prediction at each sequence position. No dropout is used. All promoter experiments use this same backbone. The differences between the base and reflow models come from the flow geometry and reflow procedure rather than from the sequence encoder.

sections.heading: Training protocol.
sections.text: For the base promoter model, we train with Adam using learning rate 5 × 10 5\times 10 , β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , and no weight decay. The batch size is 256 256 , and training runs for 200,000 200{,}000 optimization steps with gradient clipping at global norm 100 100 and random seed 42 42 . We do not use learning-rate warmup or exponential moving average. Validation is performed every 5,000 5{,}000 steps using the corresponding flow-matching objective on the validation split, and checkpoints are saved periodically. For ReSFlow, we perform a single reflow stage on top of the base model. The reflow model is initialized from the base checkpoint and fine-tuned rather than trained from scratch. We generate 100,000 100{,}000 recoupled endpoint pairs by ODE sampling from prior samples, integrating the learned vector field from t = 0 t=0 to t = 1 t=1 with batch size 128 128 and tolerances atol = rtol = 10 \mathrm{atol}=\mathrm{rtol}=10 . During reflow pair generation, the CAGE condition c c is kept fixed: for each conditioned prior sample ( x 0 , c ) (x_{0},c) , we integrate the conditional vector field to obtain the paired endpoint x 1 x_{1} . The resulting recoupled dataset therefore consists of triples ( x 0 , x 1 , c ) (x_{0},x_{1},c) . The reflow stage is trained for 100,000 100{,}000 optimization steps with batch size 128 128 and learning rate 10 10 .

sections.heading: E.5 Evaluation Metrics, NFE, and Sampling Protocols
sections.text: We describe the evaluation metrics and sampling protocols used in the main experiments. Since our model represents categorical variables as points on the probability simplex and performs flow matching after the square-root embedding, we distinguish likelihood-based evaluation, sample-quality evaluation, and task-specific downstream evaluation.

sections.heading: Negative log-likelihood.
sections.text: For the Swiss-roll experiment, we report negative log-likelihood (NLL) using the continuous-time change-of-variables formula associated with the learned ODE. This evaluation treats the data as samples from a continuous density on the simplex, or equivalently on the positive orthant of the sphere after the square-root map. Therefore, unlike discrete cross-entropy, the resulting NLL is a differential likelihood quantity and is not constrained to be non-negative. Accurate NLL estimation requires numerical integration of the learned dynamics, and we therefore evaluate NLL only with adaptive ODE integration rather than with one-step sampling.

sections.heading: Fréchet Inception Distance.
sections.text: For binarized MNIST, we report Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) as a sample-quality metric. Generated binary images are compared with the reference data distribution using the standard FID protocol; lower values indicate that the generated samples better match the real data distribution. We report FID both under adaptive ODE sampling and under one-step sampling. sections.text: For conditional promoter sequence design, we use signal proxy mean squared error (SP-MSE). Each generated promoter sequence is evaluated by a pre-trained sequence-to-function predictor, and the predicted promoter activity is compared with that of real human promoter sequences on the test chromosomes. Denoting by r i r_{i} the predicted activity profile of the real promoter and by r ^ i \widehat{r}_{i} the predicted activity profile of the generated promoter under the same conditioning signal, SP-MSE is computed as SP ​ - ​ MSE = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 ‖ r ^ i − r i ‖ 2 . \mathrm{SP\mbox{-}MSE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}\left\|\widehat{r}_{i}-r_{i}\right\|_{2}. sections.heading: Appendix G Limitations and Broader Impact
sections.text: While our manifold-based formulation successfully captures the intrinsic geometry of discrete data, it relies on model assumptions that may be violated in complex real-world scenarios. For example, the Fisher–Rao geometry inherently assumes semantic equidistance—treating all categorical states symmetrically without prior semantic bias. In reality, discrete tokens (e.g., words or subwords) possess rich, hierarchical semantic proximity (e.g., “cat” is conceptually closer to “dog” than to “apple”). While our method prevents the geometric distortion seen in continuous embedding methods (like ReDi), it does not currently incorporate pre-existing semantic priors. The assumption that pure statistical distances are sufficient may limit performance on tasks where capturing pre-trained semantic correlations is crucial. ReSFlow is a foundational methodological contribution to generative modeling on the probability simplex, and is not tied to any particular deployment. On the positive side, it offers a geometry-aware and sampling-efficient framework that can benefit discrete generative tasks in language, biology (e.g., DNA/protein sequences), and other scientific domains where categorical data are central, while its straightening property reduces inference cost and the associated energy footprint. On the negative side, ReSFlow shares the generic risks of all improved generative models: higher-quality and faster discrete generation could in principle be misused for disinformation or other malicious content.
